visuals.title: Where migraine happens
visuals.text: Trigeminal nerves and meningeal vessels drive the pain; the cortex produces the aura.

events.x: Take sumatriptan now, not during aura

glossary.Throbbing: Pulsating pain that beats in time with the pulse.
glossary.Pulsating: Throbbing, beating in time with the pulse.
glossary.Nausea: A feeling of wanting to vomit.
glossary.Sensory sensitivity: Discomfort with normal light, sound or smell during an attack.
glossary.Sleep deprivation: Not getting enough sleep; a migraine trigger.
glossary.Trimester: One of the three roughly 3-month periods of pregnancy.
glossary.Hormonal fluctuation: Rising and falling levels of hormones such as oestrogen, which can trigger migraine.
glossary.Oral contraceptives: Hormonal contraceptive pills taken by mouth.
glossary.Stroke: Brain damage from a blocked or burst blood vessel.
glossary.Contraindicated: Should not be used because the risk of harm outweighs benefit.
glossary.Differential: Another diagnosis that could explain the same symptoms.
glossary.Positional headache: Headache that changes with posture, such as lying down or standing.
glossary.Neurological deficit: Loss of function in part of the nervous system, such as weakness or visual loss.
glossary.Gold standard: The most accurate, definitive way to make a diagnosis.
glossary.Clinical diagnosis: A diagnosis made from history and examination without needing tests.
glossary.Imaging: Scans such as CT or MRI that take pictures inside the body.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen or aspirin.
glossary.Ibuprofen: An NSAID painkiller used with a triptan in acute migraine.
glossary.Aspirin: An NSAID painkiller; 900 mg can be used for acute migraine.
glossary.Paracetamol: A simple painkiller, first line in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
glossary.Ischaemic heart disease: Narrowed coronary arteries reducing blood flow to the heart; triptans can worsen it.
glossary.Peripheral vascular disease: Narrowing of arteries to the limbs, causing reduced blood flow.
glossary.Dopamine antagonist: A drug that blocks dopamine receptors; used to stop nausea and vomiting.
glossary.OTC: Over the counter: medicines bought without a prescription.
glossary.CGRP inhibitor: A drug that blocks calcitonin gene-related peptide, a key driver of migraine pain.
glossary.Asthma: Chronic airway disease with reversible narrowing; beta-blockers can trigger bronchospasm.
glossary.Raynaud's: Fingers and toes turning white then blue with cold, from vessel spasm; worsened by beta-blockers.
glossary.Comorbid: Existing at the same time as another condition.
glossary.Childbearing age: The years when a woman can become pregnant.
glossary.Menstrual-related migraine: Migraine attacks linked to the menstrual cycle, often around the period.
glossary.Neuropeptides: Small protein messengers released by nerves, such as CGRP.
glossary.Vasoactive: Able to widen or narrow blood vessels.
glossary.Meningeal vessels: Blood vessels in the meninges, the membranes covering the brain.
glossary.Depolarisation: A change in a cell's electrical charge that fires a nerve signal.
glossary.Glial: Relating to support cells of the nervous system.
glossary.Cortex: The outer layer of the brain, handling vision, sensation and speech.
glossary.Nociceptors: Nerve endings that detect painful stimuli.
glossary.Sensitisation: Nerves become more responsive, so pain is felt more easily.
glossary.Cutaneous allodynia: Pain from normally painless touch on the skin, such as brushing hair.
glossary.5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists: Drugs that stimulate these serotonin receptors, narrowing cranial vessels and blocking neuropeptide release.
glossary.Serotonin: A chemical messenger (5-HT) in the brain and gut; triptans act on its receptors.
glossary.Cranial: Relating to the skull or head.
